## Overview

- Surface anatomy and functional segmentation of the liver
- Portal venous and hepatic venous systems
- Caudate lobe (Segment I) anatomy
- Intrahepatic and extrahepatic biliary anatomy
- Biliary ductal anomalies and variations
- Gallbladder and cystic duct anomalies
- Bile duct blood supply
- Surgical exposure techniques
- Extrahepatic arterial vasculature

---

## Liver Surface Anatomy: Lobes

- **Two main lobes**: large right lobe and smaller left lobe
- Line of fusion on upper surface follows attachment of **falciform ligament**
- Inferior extent: **ligamentum teres** enters the **umbilical fissure**

::: {.fragment}
**Inferior surface (right lobe):**

- **Quadrate lobe**: anterior to transverse hilar fissure; limited by umbilical fissure (left) and gallbladder fossa (right)
- **Caudate lobe**: posterior to hilar fissure; hugs the IVC
:::

---

## Posterior Liver & IVC Relations

- IVC lies in a deep groove within the **bare area**
- Hepatic veins (RHV, MHV, LHV) open directly into the IVC
- Right suprarenal gland adjacent to IVC; adrenal vein drains into IVC
- Remainder of bare area contacts diaphragm directly
- **Ligament of the vena cava**: fibrous tissue passing posteriorly from liver edge toward vertebrae
  - Must be divided for IVC and right hepatic vein exposure
  - Up to 50% of patients: replaced by hepatic tissue; caudate may encircle IVC

---

## Functional Internal Anatomy

- Three main hepatic veins within scissurae divide liver into **four sectors**
- Each sector receives a **portal pedicle**
- **Main portal scissura**: contains middle hepatic vein
  - Runs from middle of gallbladder bed anteriorly to left of vena cava posteriorly
- Divides liver into **right liver** and **left liver** — independent in:
  - Portal venous inflow
  - Arterial supply
  - Biliary drainage

---

## Sectoral Division

- Right and left livers each divided into two by remaining portal scissurae
- **Four subdivisions** = sectors (Couinaud) / segments (Goldsmith & Woodburne)
- **Right portal scissura**: separates right liver into
  - **Anteromedial (anterior) sector**
  - **Posterolateral (posterior) sector**
- With body supine, this scissura is almost in the frontal plane

---

## Portal Venous System: Bifurcation

- **Main portal vein (MPV)** bifurcates into:
  - **Left portal vein (LPV)**
  - **Right portal vein (RPV)**
- RPV bifurcates shortly into:
  - **Right anterior portal vein (RAPV)**
  - **Right posterior portal vein (RPPV)**
- LPV has a **longer horizontal course** within the hilar plate

---

## Left Portal Pedicle & Segment IV

- Portal triad crosses **3–4 cm beneath segment IV**
- Embraced in peritoneal sheath at upper end of gastrohepatic ligament
- Separated from segment IV undersurface by connective tissue (**hilar plate**)
- Prolongation turns anteriorly/caudally within **umbilical fissure**
- Branches supply:
  - Segment **II** first
  - Then segment **III**
  - Recurrent ("feedback") branches to segment **IV**

---

## Segment IV Subdivision

- Segment IV can be separated into:
  - **Segment IVa** (superiorly)
  - **Segment IVb** (inferiorly)
- This arrangement mimics distribution to segments **V** and **VIII** on the right side
- Umbilical vein provides drainage of at least parts of segment IVb after middle hepatic vein ligation

---

## Caudate Lobe (Segment I): Position

- **Dorsal portion** of liver lying posteriorly
- Embraces the **retrohepatic IVC**
- **Constantly present left portion** + **variable right portion**
- Left side: between IVC posteriorly and left portal triad inferiorly; IVC and MHV/LHV superiorly
- Anterior surface covered by posterior surface of segment IV
- Limit: oblique plane from left portal vein to left hepatic vein

---

## Caudate Lobe: Unique Relations

- Gastrohepatic (lesser) omentum separates left caudate from segments II/III
- Caudate lies within **lesser sac** of peritoneum
- **Caudate process**: traverses to right between LPV and IVC, fusing with right lobe
- Right portion adjacent to segment IX (authors note limited clinical significance)

---

## Caudate Lobe: Vascularization & Drainage

**Portal supply:**

- Right portion (including caudate process): predominantly from RPV or MPV bifurcation
- Left portion: almost exclusively from left branch of portal vein

**Arterial/Biliary:**

- Right portion: right posterior sectional vessels
- Left portion: left main vessels

**Hepatic venous drainage:**

- **Unique**: only segment draining **directly into IVC**
- Short hepatic veins drain to anterior/left aspect of vena cava
- May drain posteriorly if significant retrocaval component

---

## Surgical Principles of Hepatic Resection

- Depend on control of:
  - **Inflow** vasculature and draining bile ducts
  - **Outflow** hepatic veins
- Remnant liver must have:
  - Excellent portal venous inflow
  - Hepatic arterial supply
  - Biliary drainage
  - **Unimpeded hepatic venous outflow**

---

## Intrahepatic Biliary Anatomy: General

- Right and left livers drained by right and left hepatic ducts
- Caudate lobe drained by several ducts joining both systems
- Intrahepatic ducts are tributaries of corresponding hepatic ducts
- Part of major portal triads penetrating liver, invaginating Glisson capsule at hilum
- **Bile ducts** usually located **above** corresponding portal branches
- **Hepatic arterial branches** situated **inferiorly** to veins

---

## Left Hepatic Ductal System

- **Left hepatic duct** drains segments II, III, and IV (constituting left liver)
- Segment III duct located slightly behind left horn of umbilical recess
- Joined by tributary from **segment IVb**
- Ducts of left lobe located **above** left branch of portal vein
- Corresponding artery situated **below** the vein

---

## Hepatic Artery Variations

Classic description found in only ~**60%** of patients.

**Common variations:**

- **Replaced common hepatic artery** arising from superior mesenteric trunk
- **Accessory right hepatic artery** from SMA (~25% of individuals)
  - Courses upward in groove posterolateral to CBD
  - Appears medial side of Calot's triangle, usually behind cystic duct

---

## Cystic Duct Anatomy

- Arises from neck or infundibulum of gallbladder
- Lumen: approximately **1–3 mm**
- Mucosa arranged in spiral folds: **valves of Heister**
- Joins common hepatic duct in **supraduodenal segment** (80%)
- May extend to **retroduodenal** or **retropancreatic** area
- Rarely joins right hepatic duct or right hepatic sectional duct

---

## Gallbladder Anomalies

- **Agenesis** (rare)
- **Bilobar gallbladders** with single cystic duct but two fundi
- **Duplication** with two cystic ducts
- **Double cystic duct** draining unilocular gallbladder
- **Congenital diverticulum** with muscular wall
- **Anomalous position**: intrahepatic (surrounded by liver tissue) or left-sided

---

## Cystic Duct Union Variations

- **Angular union**: most frequent (**75%**)
- **Parallel course**: to common hepatic duct (**20%**), with connective tissue ensheathing both
- **Spiral union**: cystic duct approaches CBD in spiral fashion
- **Absence of cystic duct**: probably acquired anomaly (cholecystocholedochal fistula)

---

## Cystic Artery Variations

Main variations include:

- Typical course
- Double cystic artery
- Crossing anterior to main bile duct
- Originating from right branch of hepatic artery, crossing common hepatic duct anteriorly
- Originating from left branch of hepatic artery
- Originating from gastroduodenal artery
- Originating from celiac axis
- Originating from replaced right hepatic artery

---

## Biliary Confluence: Normal vs. Anomalous

- **"Normal" confluence** (right + left hepatic ducts): only **72%** of patients.

- **Variations:**
  - **Triple confluence** (ra + rp + lh): **12%**
  - Right sectional duct joins main bile duct   directly: **20%**
    - Right anterior sectional: **16%**
    - Right posterior sectional: **4%**
  - Right sectional duct joins left hepatic duct:   **6%**
    - Posterior duct: **5%**
    - Anterior duct: **1%**

---

## Additional Hilar Ductal Variations

- **Absence of hepatic duct confluence**: **3%**
- Right posterior sectional duct joins neck of gallbladder or entered by cystic duct: **2%**
- Very low insertion of right sectional duct into common hepatic duct
- Cystic duct draining into right sectional duct (uncommon but important)

---

## Intrahepatic Ductal Variations

**Right side:**

- Ectopic drainage of segment V: **9%**
- Ectopic drainage of segment VI: **14%**
- Ectopic drainage of segment VIII: **20%**

**Left side:**

- Classic distribution: **67%**
- Common union between ducts of segments III and IV: **25%**
- Duct of segment IV joins common hepatic duct independently: **2%**

---

## Subvesical Duct

- Described in **20–50%** of cases
- Sometimes deeply embedded in cystic plate
- Joins common hepatic duct or right hepatic duct
- **Does not** drain specific liver territory
- **Never** communicates with gallbladder
- **Not** a satellite of portal vein or hepatic artery branch
- Injury during cholecystectomy may lead to postoperative biliary fistula if cystic plate not preserved

---

## Ectopic Drainage into Gallbladder/Cystic Duct

Variations include drainage of:

- Cystic duct into biliary confluence
- Cystic duct into left hepatic duct (no biliary confluence)
- Segment VI duct into cystic duct
- Right posterior sectional duct into cystic duct
- Distal right posterior sectional duct into neck of gallbladder
- Proximal right posterior sectional duct into body of gallbladder

---

## Bile Duct Blood Supply: Segments

Bile duct divided into three segments:

1. **Hilar**
2. **Supraduodenal**
3. **Retropancreatic**

**Supraduodenal duct:**

- Essentially **axial** blood supply
- Most vessels arise from:
  - Superior pancreaticoduodenal artery
  - Right branch of hepatic artery
  - Cystic artery
  - Gastroduodenal artery
  - Retroduodenal artery

---

## Axial Vasculature of Supraduodenal Duct

- Average of **8 small arteries** (~0.3 mm diameter)
- **3 o'clock and 9 o'clock arteries** run along lateral and medial borders
- **60%** run upward from major inferior vessels
- **38%** run downward from right hepatic artery branch and other vessels
- Only **2%** non-axial, arising directly from hepatic artery trunk

---

## Hilar & Retropancreatic Blood Supply

**Hilar ducts:**

- Copious arterial supply from surrounding vessels
- Rich network on duct surface in continuity with supraduodenal plexus

**Retropancreatic CBD:**

- Supply from **retroduodenal artery**
- Multiple small vessels form mural plexus around duct

**Venous drainage:**

- Satellites to corresponding arteries
- **3 o'clock and 9 o'clock veins** along common biliary channel
- Gallbladder veins empty into this system (not directly into portal vein)

---

## Biliary Exposure: Plate System

Fusion of Glisson capsule with connective tissue sheaths constitutes:

- **Hilar plate**: above biliary confluence
- **Cystic plate**: related to gallbladder
- **Umbilical plate**: above umbilical portion of left portal vein

---

## Lowering the Hilar Plate

**Technique (Hepp and Couinaud):**

- Lift segment IV upward
- Incise Glisson capsule at its base
- Separate upper surface of hilar plate from hepatic parenchyma
- Display hepatic duct convergence (always extrahepatic)

**Value:**

- Excellent exposure of **extrahepatic left hepatic duct** (long course beneath IV)
- Less effective for right duct (short extrahepatic segment)
- Major importance for identification of proximal mucosa during bile duct repair

---

## Combined Exposure Technique

- Simultaneous opening of:
  - Deepest portion of **gallbladder fossa**
  - **Umbilical fissure**
- Provides good exposure of biliary confluence and **right hepatic duct**
- Often avoids necessity for full hepatotomy

---

## Umbilical Fissure & Segment III Approach

- **Round ligament** (obliterated umbilical vein) runs through umbilical fissure to left portal vein
- At junction: elongations containing channels of left portal system course into liver
- Bile ducts of left lobe located **above** left portal vein branch
- Corresponding artery **below** the vein

---

## Segment III Ductal Exposure

**Steps:**

1. Dissect round ligament on its **left side**
2. Divide one or two vascular elongations of segment III
3. Display pedicle or anterior branch of **segment III duct**

**Alternative:**

- Split normal liver tissue just **left of umbilical fissure**
- Widen fissure for ductal access
- No need to divide portal blood supply to segment III

**In biliary obstruction:**

- Dilated segment III duct easily located above left branch of portal vein

---

## Segment III Hepaticojejunostomy

- Division of left horn of umbilical recess (including segment III portal vein branches)
- Exposure and opening of segment III duct
- Anastomosis to **Roux-en-Y loop of jejunum**
- Useful when standard approaches to hilum are impossible

---

## Surgical Approaches to Right Hepatic Ducts

- Exposure more hazardous than left due to lack of precise landmarks
- **Anterior sectional duct** and branches run on **left side** of corresponding portal vein
- Technique:
  - Open end of liver scissura (contains right branch of portal vein)
  - Display anterior sectional duct on left aspect of vein
  - Open dilated duct longitudinally
  - Sew to Roux-en-Y loop
- Rarely used; may be valuable in selected cases of hilar cholangiocarcinoma

---

## Exposure by Liver Resection

- **Left lobe**: amputate segment to expose segment II or III ducts
- **Right lobe**: similar procedure after removing inferior tip
- **Segment IV removal**: exposes biliary confluence
- Represents extension of mobilization after opening principal scissura and umbilical fissure

---

## Extrahepatic Vasculature: Celiac Axis

- Classic description of arterial supply found in only ~**60%** of patients
- Right and left hepatic arteries:
  - Right hepatic artery in right of hilus
  - Left hepatic artery in left of hilus
- Supply liver, biliary system, and pancreas

---

## Left Liver Biliary-Vascular Anatomy

- Segment III duct located **above** corresponding portal venous branch
- Left portal vein branch deep to duct
- Left hepatic artery branch inferior to vein
- Relationship constant and predictable for segment III approach

---

## Key Takeaways

- Liver segmentation based on **portal venous inflow** and **hepatic venous outflow** planes
- **Caudate lobe** has unique direct venous drainage to IVC
- Biliary anatomy highly variable: "normal" confluence in only 72%
- **Subvesical duct** and ectopic intrahepatic ducts pose operative risks
- **Hilar plate lowering** and **segment III approach** are critical exposure techniques
- Bile duct blood supply is **axial** — preserve 3 and 9 o'clock vessels
- Hepatic artery variations common; preoperative awareness essential
